# Chapter 6: Linear Regression with tidymodels

## From Data Exploration to Modelling

In previous chapters, we used `dplyr` and `ggplot2` to explore insurance data.

We now take the next step:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\text{Inspect} \rightarrow \text{Transform} \rightarrow \text{Summarize} \\
\rightarrow \text{Visualize} \rightarrow \text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Evaluate}
\end{gathered}
}
$$


The goal is to use the patterns in the data to build a model for **insurance charges**.

## Why Linear Regression?

Linear regression provides a simple introduction to statistical modelling.

It allows us to:

* describe relationships between variables;
* estimate model parameters;
* make predictions for new observations;
* examine prediction errors; and
* introduce ideas used in more advanced models.

We begin with **simple linear regression** and then extend it to **multiple linear regression**.

## Insurance Charges Data

We use the `insurance` dataset stored in the project's `data/` folder.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

insurance <- read_csv("../data/insuranceKaggle.csv")

glimpse(insurance)
```

The response variable will be:

$$
\boxed{\texttt{charges}}
$$

Potential predictors include:

| Variable   | Type        | Description          |
| :--------- | :---------- | :------------------- |
| `age`      | Numeric     | Age of policyholder  |
| `sex`      | Categorical | Sex                  |
| `bmi`      | Numeric     | Body mass index      |
| `smoker`   | Categorical | Smoking status       |
| `region`   | Categorical | Residential region   |
| `children` | Numeric     | Number of dependents |

## Response and Predictors

In regression, we distinguish between:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Predictor variables}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{Response variable}
}
$$


For our insurance data:

* **Response:** `charges`
* **Predictors:** `age`, `sex`, `bmi`, `smoker`, `region`, `children`

Our initial question is:

> How can we use policyholder characteristics to predict insurance charges?


## Explore Before Modelling

Before fitting a model, we examine the relationship between `charges` and potential predictors.

- **Numeric predictor:** scatter plot
- **Categorical predictor:** boxplot

---

## Insurance Charges vs. Age

```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = age, y = charges)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) + 
  labs(
    title = "Insurance Charges by Age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Charges"
  )
```



## Age and Charges

The plot suggests a **positive association** between age and charges.

Older policyholders tend to have higher charges, but there is substantial variation among individuals of the same age.

This suggests that:

$$
\text{Age explains some, but not all, variation in charges.}
$$


## BMI and Charges

```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = bmi, y = charges)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(
    title = "Insurance Charges by BMI",
    x = "BMI",
    y = "Charges"
  )
```

---

## BMI and Charges: Observations

* There appears to be a positive association between `bmi` and `charges`.
* The relationship is less clear than for `age`.

---

## Smoker and Charges

```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = smoker, y = charges)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(
    title = "Insurance Charges by Smoking Status",
    x = "Smoker",
    y = "Charges"
  )
```

---

## Smoker and Charges: Observations

* There is a substantial difference in charges between smokers and non-smokers.
* This suggests that `smoker` may be an important predictor of `charges`.


## Other Categorical Predictors: Sex

```{r}
#| label: fig-sex
#| fig-cap: "Insurance charges by sex."
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = sex, y = charges)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)
```

---

## Other Categorical Predictors: Region

```{r}
#| label: fig-region
#| fig-cap: "Insurance charges by region."
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = region, y = charges)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)
```

---

## Key Takeaways on Predictors

* The marginal relationships for `sex` and `region` appear weaker.

**Important Note:**

> A weak marginal relationship does not necessarily imply that a predictor is unimportant in a multiple regression model.


## Initial Assessment

Our visual exploration gives an initial indication of the potential predictors.

| Predictor  | Initial assessment         |
| :--------- | :------------------------- |
| `age`      | Positive association       |
| `bmi`      | Positive association       |
| `smoker`   | Strong group difference    |
| `sex`      | Weak marginal relationship |
| `region`   | Weak marginal relationship |
| `children` | To be investigated         |

Visual exploration helps us formulate a model, but it is **not sufficient on its own for feature selection**.


## Distribution of Charges

Before modelling, it is useful to examine the distribution of our response variable.

```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = charges)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Insurance Charges",
    x = "Charges",
    y = "Count"
  )
```

---

## Distribution of Charges: Insights

* The distribution of `charges` is strongly **right-skewed**, with some unusually large observations.
* These observations may have a strong influence on the fitted model.

**Statistical Clarification:**

> The distribution of the response itself does **not** determine whether the assumptions of ordinary least squares are satisfied. We examine the residuals after fitting the model.




# Build and Fit a Model

## A Prediction-Focused Workflow

Our main goal is to predict insurance charges for new observations.

We therefore use the following workflow:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Split}
\rightarrow
\text{Specify}
\rightarrow
\text{Fit}
\rightarrow
\text{Predict}
\rightarrow
\text{Evaluate}
}
$$

The `tidymodels` framework provides tools for carrying out this workflow consistently.

## Why `tidymodels`?

For a simple regression, base R can fit the model directly:

```r
lm(charges ~ age, data = insurance)
```

This is perfectly valid.

In this course, we use `tidymodels` because it provides a consistent workflow that can be extended to:

* model evaluation;
* prediction;
* preprocessing;
* multiple models; and
* more advanced modelling methods.

## The `parsnip` Package

`parsnip` provides a consistent interface for specifying and fitting models.

For linear regression:


```{r}
library(tidymodels)

linear_reg()
```

This specifies the **type of model**.

At this stage, the model has not been fitted to any data.

## Model Specification and Engine

There are two separate ideas:

**Model specification**

```r
linear_reg()
```

describes the type of model.

**Model engine**

```r
set_engine("lm")
```

specifies the computational implementation.

For our model:

```{r}
lm_mod <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

lm_mod
```

The `"lm"` engine uses R's ordinary least-squares implementation.

## Fitting the Model

Suppose we use `age` to predict `charges`.

The model is

$$
\text{charges}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1\text{age}+\varepsilon.
$$

In R, the model formula is:

```r
charges ~ age
```

We fit the model using:

```{r}
lm_fit <- lm_mod %>%
  fit(charges ~ age, data = insurance)

lm_fit
```

The modelling process is therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Specify}
\rightarrow
\text{Choose engine}
\rightarrow
\text{Fit}
}
$$

## Interpreting the Fitted Model

Suppose the fitted model is

$$
\widehat{\text{charges}}
=
3165.9+257.7\,\text{age}.
$$

The coefficient of `age` is:

$$
\boxed{257.7}
$$

Thus, according to the fitted model, a one-year increase in age is associated with an estimated increase of approximately **257.7 units in charges**, on average.

For a 10-year age difference:

$$
257.7(10)=2{,}577.
$$

The predicted difference between ages 40 and 50 is therefore approximately **2,577 units**.

## The Intercept

The intercept is:

$$
\hat{\beta}_0=3165.9.
$$

It represents the predicted charge when:

$$
\text{age}=0.
$$

Although this is mathematically part of the regression equation, age 0 is outside the meaningful range of this dataset.

Therefore, the intercept has little practical interpretation here.

## Tidy Model Results

The `broom` package converts model results into a tidy data frame.

```{r}
library(broom)

tidy(lm_fit)
```

Important columns include:

| Column      | Meaning               |
| :---------- | :-------------------- |
| `term`      | Model term            |
| `estimate`  | Estimated coefficient |
| `std.error` | Standard error        |
| `statistic` | Test statistic        |
| `p.value`   | p-value               |

For our prediction-focused analysis, the `estimate` column gives the coefficients used by the fitted model.


## Visualizing the Fitted Line

We can display the observed data together with the fitted regression line.

```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: "center"

ggplot(insurance, aes(x = age, y = charges)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  labs(
    title = "Insurance Charges vs Age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Charges"
  )
```

---

## Components of the Regression Line

* The points represent the **observed charges** ($Y$).
* The line represents the **predicted charges** ($\hat{Y}$) generated from the fitted model.
* The vertical distance between any individual observation and the line is its **residual** ($e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i$).



## What Does the Plot Tell Us?

The fitted line captures the general positive relationship between age and charges.

However, there is substantial variation around the line.

This tells us that:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Age alone does not explain all variation in charges.}
}
$$

Other characteristics, such as `bmi` and `smoker`, may provide additional predictive information.

# Predictions

## Predicting Charges for New Ages

Once the model has been fitted, we can use it to predict charges for new observations.

For example:

```{r}
new_points <- tibble(
  age = c(30, 40, 50)
)

predict(
  lm_fit,
  new_data = new_points
)
```

The `.pred` column contains the predicted **mean charge** for each age.

## Confidence Intervals for the Mean

We can also obtain 95% confidence intervals for the estimated mean charges:

```{r}
predict(
  lm_fit,
  new_data = new_points,
  type = "conf_int"
)
```

The output contains:

* `.pred` — predicted mean charge;
* `.pred_lower` — lower confidence limit;
* `.pred_upper` — upper confidence limit.

## Mean Response vs Individual Prediction

A confidence interval describes uncertainty about the **mean response**.

It should not be interpreted as the likely range of charges for an individual policyholder.

For an individual future observation, we need a **prediction interval**, which is wider because it includes both:

$$
\boxed{
\text{uncertainty in the mean}
+
\text{individual variation}
}
$$

This distinction becomes important when using regression for prediction.

# From Simple to Multiple Regression

## Why Add More Predictors?

The simple model

$$
\widehat{\text{charges}}
=
\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1\text{age}
$$

uses only one predictor.

But the data contain other potentially useful variables:

$$
\texttt{bmi},\quad
\texttt{smoker},\quad
\texttt{sex},\quad
\texttt{region},\quad
\texttt{children}.
$$

A multiple regression model allows us to consider several predictors simultaneously.

## Next Step

We have followed the basic modelling workflow:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Explore}
\rightarrow
\text{Specify}
\rightarrow
\text{Fit}
\rightarrow
\text{Interpret}
\rightarrow
\text{Predict}
}
$$

The simple model shows that age is associated with insurance charges, but substantial variation remains unexplained.

Next, we extend the model to **multiple linear regression** and investigate whether additional predictors improve our predictions.
